section_summary: This section documents Allied efforts in mid-1941 to restrict Japan’s access to petroleum, mercury, manganese, molybdenum, platinum, industrial diamonds and other strategic materials. Its central document is a lengthy State Department review explaining why the United States had gradually tightened oil controls while postponing a complete embargo to gain time for rearmament and avoid provoking Japanese expansion into the Netherlands East Indies. The remaining correspondence and reports trace Japanese procurement and barter efforts across Latin America, together with British, American and local efforts to block or redirect those transactions.

subfiles.title: Garbled mercury-quantity calculation and annotation
subfiles.about: A handwritten annotation attempts to reconcile garbled quantities and values in a mercury telegram.
subfiles.summary: The writer calculates tonnage and monetary values associated with flasks of mercury. The note warns that the underlying telegram is garbled and records an approximate value of £180–£200 per flask and a flask weight of about 96 pounds.

subfiles.title: Telegram on mercury aboard SS Mar Cantabrico
subfiles.about: Reports a large mercury shipment routed from Cádiz through Buenos Aires for Mitsui in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: SS Mar Cantabrico reportedly left Cádiz on July 25 carrying 120 tons of mercury consigned to Mitsui and Company in Tokyo. A British certificate and a Seville consular report give inconsistent quantities, reinforcing the accompanying concern that the figures were garbled.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on diesel oil for Japanese vessels in Peru
subfiles.about: Assesses whether Peru’s revised bunkering rules adequately prevent Japanese ships from obtaining excess fuel.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum discusses a Santiago report concerning 1,500 tons of diesel oil and a related Lima despatch on tighter Peruvian bunkering controls. It concludes that most of the oil was probably intended for bunkers and that the new rules limiting fuel to the next ordinary port of call offered adequate protection, so no further action appeared necessary.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Peruvian diesel-oil sale to Japanese ships
subfiles.about: Reports a Peruvian government sale of diesel oil to the Japanese ships Kunikawa and Norfolk Maru.
subfiles.summary: The Peruvian Government reportedly arranged to sell 2,000 tons of diesel oil to the Japanese vessels Kunikawa and Norfolk Maru. Norfolk Maru was expected to receive 1,500 tons, apparently as cargo, with delivery at the government-owned Los Cerritos oil field.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Naval Attaché report on Peruvian bunkering restrictions
subfiles.doc_type: paraphrased naval telegram with routing sheet
subfiles.to: U.S. naval and State Department officials
subfiles.about: Explains Peru’s inspection and approval requirements for supplying oil to Japanese ships.
subfiles.summary: The Peruvian Government would provide no oil to Japanese vessels without approval from the Ministry of War and an inspection by the captain of the port. Approved vessels would receive only enough fuel to reach the next fueling port, and ships refusing inspection would receive none.

subfiles.title: British Embassy letter on manganese exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Describes the tightening of British restrictions on manganese exports from India and Malaya to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Pre-crisis monthly quotas had allowed 10,000 tons from India and 1,700 tons from Malaya, after which both were cut by half. Following the freezing measures, export licenses from the British Empire to Japan were generally denied except for narrow compensatory transactions, and little or no Indian manganese was then moving to Japan. Malayan restrictions were complicated by Japanese ownership of the mines.

subfiles.title: Finletter letter to Will Clayton on mica shipments
subfiles.about: Promises to raise the serious issue of Indian mica shipments to Japan with the British Embassy.
subfiles.summary: Finletter acknowledges Clayton’s July 17 letter about mica exports from India to Japan. He agrees that the matter is serious and says he will take it up immediately with the British Embassy.

subfiles.title: Oil Shipments to Japan: A Survey of This Government’s Policy
subfiles.about: Reviews the political, strategic, legal and economic reasoning behind the gradual restriction of American oil shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum traces American Far Eastern policy from Japan’s seizure of Manchuria through the war in China, the European war and Japan’s expansion toward French Indochina. It explains that public opposition to sanctions, treaty and commercial-law concerns, the need for cooperation from other oil producers and military warnings against simultaneous Atlantic and Pacific wars initially militated against a complete embargo. Washington instead imposed licensing controls, stopped aviation-gasoline exports, strengthened American, British and Dutch defenses and aided China while gaining time for rearmament. By mid-1941, Japan’s worsening strategic position and the German attack on the Soviet Union made stronger measures, including asset freezing and a possible oil embargo, less likely to trigger an immediate seizure of the Netherlands East Indies.

subfiles.title: Code radiogram on Japanese troop movements near Canton and Hong Kong
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese troop strength near Canton and Hong Kong and movements toward Cambodia.
subfiles.summary: Most of the Japanese 18th Division reportedly remained near Canton and Hong Kong. British sources estimated that approximately one division had moved from the Canton area to Cambodia, together with about one brigade of the 104th Division.

subfiles.title: Senator Thomas letter requesting an answer for Parke S. Petterson
subfiles.about: Requests a State Department response to a constituent’s questions about American policy toward Japan.
subfiles.summary: Senator Thomas forwards a letter from his constituent Parke S. Petterson of Salt Lake City. He asks Green to prepare an appropriate reply explaining national policy toward Japan.

subfiles.title: Parke S. Petterson letter criticizing supplies to Japan
subfiles.about: Challenges Senator Thomas to explain continued American exports of oil, scrap iron and munitions to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Petterson accuses Thomas and other policymakers of appeasing Japan and enabling its war against China through shipments of strategic materials. He questions why exports continued after Japan aligned with Hitler and Mussolini and while the United States was building its own defenses. He asks for a clear explanation without requesting disclosure of confidential policy.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Thomas on exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Responds to Petterson’s criticism by outlining existing restrictions and the recent change in oil policy.
subfiles.summary: The reply rejects the claim that militarily important goods had flowed unrestrictedly to Japan, stating that exports had been limited to prewar quantities and were being curtailed further. It notes the virtual embargo on scrap iron and steel since October 16, 1940, and cites the President’s explanation that earlier oil shipments had helped preserve peace in the Pacific. A copy of the President’s August 1 announcement and Petterson’s letter were enclosed.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with George S. Walden on petroleum exports
subfiles.about: Records guidance given to Standard-Vacuum concerning petroleum shipments from the Netherlands East Indies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hiss informed Walden that Dutch arrangements for payment in guilders eliminated the immediate issue of releasing Japanese blocked dollar balances, although they also preserved Japan’s dollar holdings. The Netherlands Indies Government was expected to align its export licensing with American policy, but the Department would not guarantee that misunderstandings could not occur. Standard-Vacuum was given a list of products completely embargoed by the United States, allowed to resume license applications for its normal-quota business and encouraged to coordinate its position with Shell.

subfiles.title: Representative Mahon letter concerning proposed Mexican-Japanese barter
subfiles.about: Requests an authoritative ruling on a constituent’s plan to exchange Mexican oil for Japanese silk.
subfiles.summary: Mahon forwards Andrew A. Bradford’s proposal for Mexico to barter oil and petroleum products for Japanese silk. Bradford also wished to know whether he or an organization he formed could participate in such transactions on behalf of the Mexican Government with State Department approval.

subfiles.title: Andrew A. Bradford letter proposing oil-for-silk barter
subfiles.about: Proposes supervised Mexican barter with Japan to relieve shortages of silk and rayon.
subfiles.summary: Bradford relays a Mexican associate’s warning that shortages of natural and artificial silk could leave thousands of textile workers unemployed. He proposes that Mexico exchange crude or refined oil for Japanese silk and rayon, possibly sending half the silk to the United States. If imports into the United States were unacceptable, he asks whether Mexico could trade directly with Japan under American supervision and whether he could help arrange the transactions.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull reply to George Mahon on Mexican trade with Japan
subfiles.about: Declines to encourage Bradford’s proposed Mexican barter trade with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull explains that sovereign Mexico needs no American permission for foreign trade except where frozen funds are involved, but the United States was not seeking Japanese silk through Mexico. He observes that Mexico had shown little desire to sell petroleum to Japan and lacked practical West Coast loading facilities, while Gulf Coast transport would be costly. The Department therefore could not encourage the proposal, although it was attempting to help Mexico obtain rayon and avert textile unemployment.

subfiles.title: Mexican Union Refuses Japanese Offer of Silk
subfiles.about: Reports that a Mexican textile union rejected a Japanese silk-for-war-supplies proposal.
subfiles.summary: Japanese importers offered to meet Mexico’s silk and rayon needs in exchange for renewed shipments of war supplies to Japan. The Textile Workers’ Union rejected the offer, prioritizing Mexico’s continental-defense commitments, and instead asked the government to seek supplies from the United States to protect 7,000 jobs.

subfiles.title: Memorandum citing J. H. Carmical’s estimates of Japanese oil stocks
subfiles.about: Extracts published estimates of Japan’s oil imports, reserves and endurance.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum cites a New York Times article stating that Japan imported 13.5 million barrels of crude oil from the United States and 4.25 million from other sources in the preceding year. Carmical estimated Japanese stocks at roughly 80 million barrels, sufficient for about two and one-half years, with most of the supply having come from the United States.

subfiles.title: British Embassy letter on Peruvian molybdenum
subfiles.about: Reports that Peruvian molybdenum deliveries to Japan will stop if Britain purchases the output.
subfiles.summary: A telegram from Lima stated that all further molybdenum deliveries to Japan would cease provided the United Kingdom bought the material instead. Because the British Government had already agreed to purchase it, Marris considered the matter satisfactorily concluded.

subfiles.title: Finletter letter forwarding the molybdenum settlement
subfiles.about: Forwards the British report that the Peruvian molybdenum problem had been resolved.
subfiles.summary: Finletter sends Bridgman a copy of Marris’s September 4 letter. He states that it appears to dispose of the problem of Peruvian molybdenum.

subfiles.title: British Embassy letter on a proposed Mexican mercury shipment to Shanghai
subfiles.about: Requests investigation of an apparent attempt to circumvent controls on Mexican mercury exports.
subfiles.summary: British information from Shanghai indicated an effort to import 11,400 pounds of Mexican mercury, probably for Japanese account, at a large price premium. The transaction involved a possible supplier associated with Liborio Benítez, an intermediary named Malcolm and an unknown Shanghai concern called AGMOL, which established a $30,000 credit in Mexico City. Reid-Adam asks whether the scheme would violate or evade the United States-Mexican agreement limiting mercury exports.

subfiles.title: Braden telegram on Colombian silk and platinum
subfiles.about: Urges rapid action to supply Colombian textile mills and conclude the purchase of Colombian platinum.
subfiles.summary: The Colombian Government estimated quarterly silk-mill requirements at 44,418 pounds, with only 31,532 pounds in stock, and warned that conversion to rayon would take time. Braden requested either evidence disproving those claims or assurances of rayon supplies so plants would not close. He also urged immediate purchase of 62,376 grams of platinum and dispatch of a Metals Reserve Company representative, warning that buyers in Argentina and Cuba were already making offers.

subfiles.title: Statistics on U.S. petroleum exports to Japan, 1937–1941
subfiles.about: Calculates American exports of primary petroleum products to Japan from 1937 through early 1941.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum totals major petroleum exports to Japan during 1937–1940 at 109.178 million barrels, excluding several minor categories. The accompanying Department of Commerce table breaks the figures down into crude oil, gasoline, gas and fuel oil, residual fuel oil and lubricating oil. A note adds that first-quarter 1941 exports totaled about 4.735 million barrels and corrects one unpublished figure upward.

subfiles.title: Buenos Aires telegram on strategic-mineral exports
subfiles.about: Reports Argentine exports of strategic minerals and large mercury and ore shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The telegram lists August exports to Japan of tungsten, mica, vanadinite, lithium and gilsonite, alongside smaller shipments to the United States and a planned 400-ton beryl shipment. It reports that Yamaura Maru carried 5,000 flasks of mercury totaling 200 tons and that Yamazatu Maru was loading tungsten and vanadinite ore. Inquiries were under way into the mercury’s origin.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Japanese funds for American cotton
subfiles.about: Points to a telegram on a Japanese plan to use frozen U.S. funds to buy American cotton.
subfiles.summary: Japanese officials meeting at Peiping reportedly decided to transfer between $600,000 and $1 million from Japanese funds in the United States to Volkart Brothers in New York. The money was intended to finance purchases of American cotton for Japanese army equipment.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on attempts to obtain industrial diamonds for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports on unsuccessful efforts to procure Mexican bortz for shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Bernard Bandler & Sons commissioned Robert H. Sherman to investigate purchasing commercial diamonds in Mexico after encountering difficulties sourcing bortz in Brazil, but his efforts failed. The firm stated that it would sell commercial diamonds domestically only when their final American use was known and that all such sales were reported to the British Board of Trade under a gentleman’s agreement.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on possible Japanese lard shipments to Germany
subfiles.about: Points to a memorandum suggesting that American lard purchased by Japan might be forwarded to Germany.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references a European Affairs memorandum dated April 2, 1941. Its subject is information indicating that lard bought by Japan in the United States may have been sent onward to Germany.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Navy inquiry into oil policy toward Japan
subfiles.about: Points to a Navy Department letter requesting information on American oil policy toward Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies the subject as policy governing oil supplied to Japan. It refers researchers to a Navy Department letter of August 9, 1941, filed elsewhere in the decimal records.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Colombian platinum and silk requirements
subfiles.about: Points to a telegram requesting an estimate of Colombia’s silk needs during a three-month adjustment period.
subfiles.summary: The referenced telegram concerns the linked Colombian platinum and silk negotiations. It requested an estimate of how much silk Colombia would need to carry its mills through a three-month adjustment period.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on cancellation of a Peruvian molybdenum contract with Japan
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch reporting that a molybdenum contract with Japan could be cancelled immediately.
subfiles.summary: The sheet refers to Peruvian despatch no. 1647, dated August 29, 1941. The underlying report stated that the molybdenum contract supplying Japan might be cancelled at once.

subfiles.title: Continuing Efforts of Japanese to Obtain Bolivian Minerals
subfiles.from: Douglas Jenkins, U.S. Legation, La Paz
subfiles.about: Describes Japanese barter, banking and intermediary schemes intended to secure Bolivian strategic minerals.
subfiles.summary: After threatening to halt textile exports, Japanese representatives proposed buying Bolivian mineral surpluses with local currency or bartering textiles and pottery for minerals, but Bolivian officials showed little interest. The Yokohama Specie Bank then sought dollar facilities through the Banco Central, while a concern owned by Armando H. Ono proposed that Jorge Saenz e Hijos exchange Japanese goods for antimony, lead, copper and quinine. Jenkins believed these schemes had largely been blocked, although Japanese retail stocks and goods at Arica temporarily softened the effect of Japan’s suspension of exports. The despatch also details indirect payment channels through banks and trading concerns in Peru, Chile, Brazil, San Francisco and New York.

subfiles.title: Routing memorandum to Yost
subfiles.from: Office of the Special Assistant to the Secretary
subfiles.about: Refers an attached matter to Yost as falling within his jurisdiction.
subfiles.summary: The brief memorandum states that the writer assumes the matter belongs within Yost’s jurisdiction. Consequently, the writer has taken no action on it.

subfiles.title: British Embassy letter on Mitsubishi well-drilling machinery
subfiles.about: Reports suspected Mitsubishi efforts to buy well-drilling machinery in Buenos Aires for eventual re-export to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The British Embassy links earlier Mitsubishi efforts in Mexico with a new Buenos Aires inquiry for four drilling machines from the National Supply Company. Mitsubishi’s Buenos Aires office sent the specifications to its Ore Department in Tokyo, suggesting that machinery nominally ordered for Argentina might later be re-exported to Japan. The page supplies prices, delivery terms and partial equipment specifications; the letter continues beyond this section.
